extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalism students; historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for assessing American newspapers (c.1914–1940), covering ownership models, editorial quality, finances, format and public-service performance with illustrative historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee ownership and control
rubrics_metrics.description: A type of ownership by which editorial and business staffs own and conduct the paper (stock-company plan, staff ownership, mutualization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kansas City Star, New York Sun, Milwaukee Journal. Implementation details discussed include issuing preferred stock on easy terms to long‑service staff, organizing a stock company of employees to buy the property, and ‘‘mutualizing’’ ownership so staff hold the stock. The text notes skepticism from experienced business men but cites financial success (e.g., Star paid off mortgage ahead of schedule). Anti-patterns: schemes predicted to fail; guidance notes use of options/trusts (see related metric) to preserve continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to preserve employee ownership continuity (options and trusts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal/financial devices to prevent staff ownership from dissipating — stock trust‑indentures, options for corporation/other stockholders to buy shares if employment ends, trusts to hold stock so it cannot be sold outside the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kansas City Star employees signed options to ensure continuation; Sun had company options to prevent outside sales; Milwaukee Journal set up a trust so stock could not be sold outside the Journal organization. Guidance emphasizes these as essential to assuring continuation of staff-ownership and preventing outside takeover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of staff and long‑tenure personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity and long-tenure staff are judged valuable — staff ownership and management practices that promote long-tenure foster stability and editorial continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites the Sun’s ownership plan 'made for continuity and a long-tenure staff' and Noyes family control of the Washington Star as furnishing 'an unusual if not unique example of continuity in eastern metropolitan journalism.' Continuity is linked to institutional prestige and consistent editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial performance and profitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper’s success measured by profits, ability to pay interest, meet payments, eliminate mortgages, and overall financial return on the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: The New York Times became 'one of the world’s greatest newspaper money‑makers'; the Star increased profits and paid off mortgage; Evening Post and Daily News are discussed in terms of losing/earning money. Indicators include advertising linage, circulation, and whether owners could invest (e.g., buy new presses). Anti-patterns: papers that 'did not respond' to format changes or that 'lost about half a million dollars a year'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and market reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured by daily and Sunday circulation numbers and growth (single‑day and national editions), including reach of predated or jackrabbit editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Times circulation figures (near 500,000), Sunday editions passing the million mark, Inquirer daily circulation up to 390,000. Circulation is repeatedly used as a metric of success and influence. Tactics to increase circulation (jackrabbit editions, tabloid sizing) are discussed under format/marketing metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising linage and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume and quality of advertising (department‑store advertising, advertising linage) as a major revenue and success indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Times 'attracted heavy department‑store advertising'; Washington Star led in daily and Sunday advertising volume; Evening Bulletin had 'much the best advertising patronage.' Advertising linage often constrained page space and influenced editorial decisions (e.g., turning down advertising for lack of space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and depth of foreign and national coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent and quality of foreign news reporting and Washington correspondence; voluminous foreign news is a mark of a paper’s stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times noted for 'voluminous foreign news' and strong Washington correspondence; Public Ledger developed a great foreign news service, much of which it syndicated. The book links expanded foreign coverage to prestige and competitive positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of important documents, speeches, and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness and practice of printing primary materials (documents, speeches) and providing indexes to contents as part of public service and record-keeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Times 'printing of important documents and speeches' and beginning 'a thorough index of its contents in 1913' are cited. Indexing is presented as an institutional practice contributing to the paper’s utility and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and political stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of independence from party lines or explicit editorial stances; papers are evaluated by whether they are independent or aligned with political positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times is praised for 'independence of party'; Evening Post kept an independent Democratic path (yet under some editors had defined partisan tones). Owner influence and political alignment (supporting or opposing candidates, engagement in political crusades) are discussed as affecting editorial character. Anti-pattern: overt owner interference or partisan vendettas undermining reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial quality and writing consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of prose and evenness of editorial standards — 'well‑written home newspaper' and 'remarkably even career of excellence' are markers of editorial quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sun under Frank M. O’Brien exemplified even, well‑written local journalism with stable circulation. Editors’ personal reputations (e.g., Rollo Ogden as a scholar) are linked to sustained editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service, crusades, and investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers judged by their public‑service campaigns, crusades against corruption, investigative exposures, and whether such work earned public honors (Pulitzer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Canton News' crusade (Pulitzer for public service), Star’s campaign for lower gas rates (led to libel suits), States' 1939 exposure leading to investigations of political heirs. Public-service journalism is framed as central to a paper’s civic role, but also risky (lawsuits, retaliation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to take legal and political risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness to pursue crusading or investigative stories despite libel suits, political retaliation, or owners’ involvement in politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Star's crusade produced record libel suits and attempts at retaliation (Doherty bought interest in competitor). Annenberg's political fights illustrate how owner actions can provoke investigations and consequences. The book treats such risks as part of vigorous local journalism but notes potential costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format, design, and feature innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of new formats and features (tabloid size, halftone illustrations, comics, departmentalization, streamlined dress) as measures of responsiveness and modernization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted innovations: increase of foreign news, use of halftone illustrations, introduction of comics, the Post's 'handsome streamlined dress' and departmentalizing of news, Times increasing from 24 to as much as 40 pages, and the coming of the modern tabloid. Success of format changes varied: some tabloid experiments failed, others succeeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing, promotions, and price strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of promotions, price changes, and ballyhoo to boost circulation and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcript's 'unusual promotional ballyhoo' and raising single‑copy price to five cents are cited; Annenberg's use of 'jackrabbit' editions to boost Sunday circulation. These moves are presented as ways to increase revenue and readership but with mixed results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner involvement and interference vs. professional management
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which owners interfere with editorial policy versus allowing professional managers/editors autonomy, and how that affects a paper’s tone and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamont 'abstained from interference' at the Evening Post and turned control to a syndicate; Thomas W. Lamont's arrangement is praised. By contrast, owners who politically intervene or use papers for vendettas (e.g., Annenberg’s battles) invite problems. Guidance: professional oversight preferred for reputation and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in plant and equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital investment in buildings, presses, and equipment as indicator of long‑term commitment and capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago Daily News' new $10,000,000 building; Curtis built and equipped a great building for the Public Ledgers at $15,000,000; Star bought $1,000,000 worth of new presses. Such investment supported news operations and signaled financial health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining separate editorial identities after consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple papers are combined under single ownership, preserving distinct editorial identities of each title is a valued practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sherman H. Bowles bought multiple Springfield papers and 'sedulously maintained the editorial identity of each paper' while selling advertising as a unit. Guidance implies editorial plurality within consolidated business structures is an acceptable model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition, awards, and editorial prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer Prizes, editorial awards, and the stature of editors are used to judge a paper’s excellence and influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Henry J. Haskell won the Pulitzer for editorial writing; Cox's Canton News received the Pulitzer for public service; newspapers and editors with scholarly reputations (e.g., Rollo Ogden) are highlighted as enhancing a paper’s standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to local market structure (consolidation into single‑paper cities)
rubrics_metrics.description: How newspapers adapt when markets consolidate (single‑ownership cities, mergers), including strategies to continue editorial service in a less-competitive environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Montgomery became a single-paper city when the Alabama Journal merged with the Advertiser; Providence consolidated under one ownership. The account discusses consolidation as a common response to economic pressures with implications for competition and pluralism.
